readings.text: Nifty 50 is 4.3% above its 200-day average, and that average is falling (-1.2% over 20 days). By the moving-average test the primary trend reads as mixed / sideways.
Over one month the Nifty 50 moved +10.7% and the Sensex +11.6%: the two indices confirm each other.
Nifty 50 RSI (14) is 79. That is above 70, the usual overbought line.
Nifty 50 MACD is above its signal line and above zero.
56% of the 758 covered stocks are above their 200-day average and 46% above their 50-day average.

Against the Nifty 50 over 3 months, the strongest sectors were Communication Services (+2.1%), Energy (-1.5%), Consumer Defensive (-1.6%); the weakest were Industrials (-7.7%), Basic Materials (-8.3%), Utilities (-8.5%).

Brent crude is down 6.3% in a month ($97.8). Falling crude lowers input costs for users such as airlines, paints and logistics and squeezes oil producers; for an importer like India it eases fuel prices and inflation.
The rupee strengthened 3.0% against the dollar in a month (₹93.89). Imports get cheaper; exporters earn fewer rupees per dollar.
The US 10-year yield is 4.88% (-35 basis points in a month). Foreign portfolio money, which NISM calls 'hot money' that can leave at any time, watches global rates.
India VIX (expected 30-day volatility of the Nifty) is 17.5, +26% in a month.

The most heavily reported world themes of the last 3 days: posts and remarks by market-moving people (16 reports), government, elections and policy (14 reports), crude oil, gas and commodities (14 reports). Conflicts in oil regions, sanctions and trade wars mainly reach Indian stocks through crude prices, the rupee and supply chains.

news.note: Collected from Google News searches, limited to a fixed list of established outlets, grouped when several outlets carry the same story, and ranked by how many outlets carry it and how recent it is. Posts on X or Truth Social appear when these outlets report them. Headlines are not summarised or checked.

trend.src: NISM Series XV (Research Analyst) workbook, §15.4 Understanding Market Trends
trend.says: A primary trend is the long movement of a year or more: bull (sustained rise), bear (prolonged decline) or sideways. 50- or 100-day averages, trendlines, MACD and higher highs / higher lows are listed as the tools to identify it.

dow.src: NISM Series XV, §15.3 The Dow Theory
dow.says: Six tenets, including: the market has three trends (primary, secondary, minor); indices must confirm each other (Nifty and Sensex should move together); volume should rise in the direction of the trend; a trend stays in force until a clear reversal.

ma.says: When the average points up the trend is up. When a stock trades at or near a rising average this could be a good time to buy, and vice versa. Price > 13 EMA > 21 EMA > 34 EMA describes an uptrend; the reverse a downtrend.

macd.says: MACD = 12-day EMA minus 26-day EMA; the signal line is its 9-day EMA. An uptrend is likely to continue while MACD is above the signal line and both are rising. The zero line separates confirmed bull and bear phases.

rsi.says: Above 70 is usually called overbought and below 30 oversold. In a bull market RSI rarely falls below 44-45; in a bear market it rarely rises above 50-55. RSI can stay overbought or oversold for long periods in strong trends.

adx.says: ADX measures trend strength, not direction. Below 25 is a weak or no trend; a rising ADX above 25 is a strong trend. +DMI above -DMI with a rising ADX is described as a buy signal; avoid crossovers when ADX is weak.

rsc.src: NISM Series XV, §15.9.5 Relative Strength Comparative
rsc.says: Compares a stock (or sector) with a benchmark such as the Nifty 50, normalised to 100: above 100 means it is outperforming, below 100 underperforming.

obv.src: NISM Series XV, §15.9.6 On Balance Volume
obv.says: OBV adds volume on up days and subtracts it on down days. It should rise with rising prices; OBV above its 20-period average with a fresh upturn is read as fresh momentum.

sr.src: NISM Series XV, §15.7 Support and Resistance
sr.says: Support is a level where a fall tends to pause, resistance where a rise tends to pause. Moving averages act as dynamic support and resistance; breakouts need volume confirmation.

commod_eq.src: NISM Series XV, §4.10 Impact of commodity market on equity market
commod_eq.says: Rising commodity prices raise input costs and squeeze margins of companies that use them; falling prices help. Rising crude helps oil producers and hurts airlines and logistics. A fall in copper may signal slowing industrial demand, dragging metal and infrastructure stocks.

intl.src: NISM Series XV, §11.4 International and domestic markets
intl.says: Crude oil prices on international exchanges directly affect fuel prices and inflation in importing countries like India. A weaker rupee makes imports more expensive and amplifies global price rises.

dollar.src: NISM Series XV, §11.3 Currency and dollar index
dollar.says: Most commodities are priced in US dollars. A stronger dollar usually reduces global demand and pushes commodity prices down; a weaker dollar supports them. Weak emerging-market currencies raise the cost of imported commodities.

macro_ind.src: NISM Series XV, §11.7 Macroeconomic indicators and commodities
macro_ind.says: Rising inflation typically pushes investors toward precious metals like gold as a hedge. Higher interest rates strengthen currencies and often reduce commodity prices.

geo.src: NISM Series XV, §11.8 Government policies and geopolitical impacts
geo.says: Conflicts in oil-producing regions often disrupt supply and lift crude prices. Trade wars and sanctions restrict the flow of energy, metals and farm goods. Tensions over shipping routes or pipelines add a risk premium.

cad.src: NISM Series XV, §5.3.6 Fiscal policy, balance of payments
cad.says: A high current account deficit weakens the currency, makes imports and capital goods dearer and foreign borrowing costlier. A weaker currency makes exports more competitive.

fpi.src: NISM Series XV, §5.3.5 FDI and FPI flows
fpi.says: Foreign portfolio money is considered 'hot money' because it can be pulled out at any time, which can create systemic risk; FDI is long-term and stable.

rates.src: NISM Series XV, §5.3.3 Inflation and interest rates
rates.says: Higher rates reduce investment and can slow the economy; real estate and auto are hit harder because buyers borrow. Higher inflation reduces discretionary income and demand across the board.

global.says: Integrated economies mean a problem in one part of the world affects other parts; the 2008 US credit crisis is the example given.

emh.src: NISM Series XXI-B (Portfolio Managers) workbook, §13.2 Efficient markets
emh.says: In the semi-strong form of market efficiency, prices already reflect all public information such as results, dividends, corporate restructuring, economic and political news, so acting on news after it is public should not give above-average risk-adjusted returns. The evidence is mixed.

bias.says: Herd mentality, confirmation bias, anchoring, loss aversion and projection bias (projecting the recent past far into the future) are listed as the main biases investors should guard against.

pe.src: NISM Series XV, §10.7.2 Price to Earnings
pe.says: All else equal, a P/E above the peer group and the market is considered expensive and below it undervalued; but companies with higher growth or lower risk should trade at a premium, and lower growth or higher risk at a discount.

peg.says: P/E divided by the growth rate. Peter Lynch's rule of thumb: below 1 may be treated as undervalued. A rule of thumb may not suit every case; compare PEG across peers.

ev.src: NISM Series XV, §10.7.4-10.7.5 EV/EBITDA and EV/Sales
ev.says: Neutral to the capital structure; lower is cheaper all else equal, with premiums for growth or lower risk. P/E and EV/EBITDA cannot be used when profits are negative; EV/Sales then helps, if a turnaround is likely.

dy.says: Dividend per share / price. A high dividend yield can look like value but may reflect limited growth avenues; compare it with company fundamentals.

pb.says: Price to book compares the price with the balance-sheet value of equity; read it together with ROE.

roe.says: ROE = profit after tax / net worth, 'the single most important parameter for an equity investor to start digging'. Higher is better. ROCE = EBIT / capital employed.

dupont.says: ROE = net margin x asset turnover x leverage. A higher ROE from margin or efficiency is a reason to cheer; from higher leverage it brings higher risk.

margin.says: EBITDA margin and PAT margin. A higher margin than peers indicates greater efficiency; a trend of rising margins means improving profitability; very high margins rarely last as competitors enter.

de.says: High debt is risky in a downturn. On a most conservative basis a debt/equity of 1 or less is the benchmark, then judge by industry, track record and capital needs.

icr.says: EBIT / interest. A high ratio is comfortable; below 1 or negative means earnings do not cover interest, and such businesses may get into significant problems if they do not turn around.

cr.says: Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities. Above 1 means current assets exceed current liabilities. Below 1 is not always a red flag: companies with bargaining power often run on customers' money.

growth.says: Investors pay higher P/E for above-average expected growth. Past trends are facts; future trends are only assumptions.

promoter.says: Track the promoter group's shareholding and its changes. Pledging is not necessarily a governance concern, but a high pledged share can aggravate falls if lenders sell.

peer.says: Ratios compared with companies of the same sector show where the company stands against peers; peer comparison is critical before any research report.

beta.says: Beta measures how much a stock tends to move with the market; above 1 moves more than the market, below 1 less.

corp.src: NISM Series XV, Chapter 9 Corporate actions
corp.says: Dividends, rights, bonus, splits, buybacks, mergers, demergers and delisting change the share count or structure and need to be read for their effect on value.

eic.src: NISM Series X-A (Investment Adviser Level 1), §8.5 Equity research and stock selection
eic.says: Fundamental analysis covers Economy, Industry and Company (E-I-C). Top-down starts with the economy, then industries, then companies; bottom-up starts with the company.
